title: Acute kidney injury: staging, the first tests, and the drugs to hold

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the KDIGO acute kidney injury guideline. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: A creatinine rise of at least how much within 48 hours defines acute kidney injury?
questions.why: Or a rise to 1.5 times baseline within seven days, or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for six hours. Small absolute rises matter because creatinine lags behind the fall in filtration.

questions.q: Stage 3 acute kidney injury means creatinine has risen to at least how many times baseline?
questions.why: Or a creatinine of 4.0 or more, or the start of dialysis. Stage 1 is 1.5 to 1.9 times and stage 2 is 2 to 2.9 times.

questions.q: Which cheap test should be done early in every acute kidney injury to exclude obstruction?
questions.a: A bladder scan and kidney ultrasound
questions.why: Obstruction is reversible if caught. A catheter for retention, or a nephrostomy for an obstructed upper tract, can restore function within days.

questions.q: A fractional excretion of sodium below what suggests a prerenal cause in a patient not on diuretics?
questions.why: On diuretics the fractional excretion of urea is used instead, with under 35% pointing to prerenal. Contrast nephropathy and glomerulonephritis can mimic a low sodium excretion.

questions.q: Which urine finding points to acute tubular necrosis?
questions.why: Red cell casts mean glomerulonephritis, white cell casts interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis, and hyaline casts are normal. The urinalysis is the single most useful test.

questions.q: Which drugs are held during an acute kidney injury?
questions.why: Diuretics are held if the patient is volume depleted. The renin-angiotensin blocker usually restarts once function recovers, since it protects the kidney long term.

questions.q: Which drugs need dose adjustment or extra monitoring in acute kidney injury?
questions.why: Renally cleared drugs accumulate quickly. A pharmacist review on the day the injury is recognised prevents most of the harm.

questions.q: What prevents contrast-associated acute kidney injury in a high-risk patient who needs the scan?
questions.a: Intravenous isotonic fluid before and after the contrast
d: A dose of furosemide before the scan
questions.why: N-acetylcysteine has been shown not to help. The contrast volume is minimised, and NSAIDs and metformin are held around the study.

questions.q: Which antibiotic combination is associated with a higher rate of acute kidney injury than either alone?
questions.why: Cefepime is often substituted for piperacillin-tazobactam when vancomycin is needed. Aminoglycosides and amphotericin are the other classic nephrotoxins.

questions.q: Which are indications for urgent dialysis in acute kidney injury?
questions.why: Certain poisonings such as lithium and ethylene glycol complete the list. Starting dialysis early on the numbers alone did not improve outcomes in trials.

questions.q: What is the role of loop diuretics in acute kidney injury?
questions.a: Treating volume overload only; they do not treat the injury itself
d: Converting oliguric to non-oliguric injury improves survival
questions.why: Forcing urine output with diuretics does not change kidney recovery or mortality. A patient who does not respond is closer to needing dialysis.

questions.q: After an episode of acute kidney injury, when should kidney function be rechecked to look for chronic disease?
questions.why: Persistent reduction at three months meets the definition of chronic kidney disease. Even a fully recovered injury raises the long-term risk, so the episode goes on the problem list.
